newsitem.title: ITALY: Pope will have no deputy during surgery.
newsitem.headline: Pope will have no deputy during surgery.

text.p: Who runs Russia while President Boris Yeltsin awaits heart surgery may be mystifying Kremlin watchers, but there is no doubt about who is in charge at the Vatican.
Pope John Paul, who will have his appendix removed at Rome's Gemelli hospital on Tuesday, cannot be substituted if he is incapacitated by illness or otherwise impeded in his functions.
"You don't have a stand-in for the Pope," said Monsignor Adrian Toffolo, rector of the English College in Rome.

"There are things that only he can do and there isn't anyone else who can step into his shoes unless he dies or resigns, in which case the College of Cardinals would have to have a conclave to elect a new Pope."
The Pope, 76, enjoys "supreme, full, immediate and universal ordinary power in the Church" according to the Code of Canon Law which governs the workings of the Roman Catholic Church.
Canon Law also states that "when the Roman See is vacant or entirely impeded nothing is to be innovated in the governance of the universal Church".
The Pope has supreme authority on all issues of doctrine and teaching as well as in the appointment of bishops.

Day-to-day running of the Vatican's affairs lies in the hands of its Secretary of State, Cardinal Angelo Sodano, and the Holy See's various Congregations for specific Church issues conduct routine business.

During the Pope's hospitalisation, any urgent matter must be brought to Sodano's attention although he cannot take any decision which lies specifically in the Pontiff's domain. Sodano is likely to visit the Pope daily during his hospital stay.
"If certain things require the Holy Father's personal attention, they can wait," the Vatican's chief spokesman Joaquin Navarro-Valls said last month.

Responding to a reporter's question about what would happen if the Pope were, for example, to fall into a coma, he said it was a mistake to try to transpose the arrangements of secular states to the Roman Catholic Church.

The question arose during the Pope's visit to France after an Italian news magazine report, ridiculed by the Vatican, said the Pope had left sealed instructions with aides to be opened if his operation went wrong or he became mentally incapacitated.
The Pope has had major abdominal surgery three times already since 1981, twice after he was almost killed by a would-be assassin's bullet and again in 1992 to remove a colon tumour.
He has given every indication that, while beyond the normal retirement age of 75 which applies to bishops, he intends to remain Pope until his death.
There is no modern precedent for a Pope's retirement. The last Pope whom scholars agree resigned was Celestine V in 1294.

"If it should happen that the Roman Pontiff resigns his office, it is required for validity that he makes the resignation freely and that it be duly manifested, but not that it be accepted by anyone," Canon Law states.

Special norms, decreed by Pope Paul VI in 1975 and updated by John Paul II this year, apply during an interregnum on the death or resignation of a Pope. They cover only ordinary business and urgent matters pending election of a successor.
